strengths: Provides a unified and systematic expressivity theory for permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, addressing a timely and important gap in the literature.

Establishes expressive equivalence among all prominent permutation-equivariant weight-space architectures (DWS, NP-NFN, HNP-NFN, GMN, NG-GNN), with NFT as a special case under a general-position assumption. This is a strong and useful unification.

Identifies and analyzes four natural approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators), yielding a comprehensive framework for future work.

Proves universality for function-space functionals without additional assumptions, and universality for permutation-invariant functionals and permutation-equivariant operators under a mild general-position condition, with explicit edge-case counterexamples.

Characterizes the limitation of fixed architectures for function-space operators and shows that universality is recovered by allowing the input architecture to grow, which provides principled guidance for architecture design.
Includes an honest limitations discussion and clearly delineates the scope of the results (MLPs, permutation symmetries).
weaknesses: The proof of Theorem F.9 (and hence the informal Proposition 7.1) appears flawed. The argument assumes that if Ψ(f) is piecewise linear with M regions on X and agrees with the rescaled f on [a,b]^n, then for any x* outside [a,b]^n the affine extension must equal f((x*-a)/(b-a)). This does not follow: the affine extension of a region from [a,b]^n to X can legitimately differ from the rescaled f at x*, so the claimed contradiction is not established. This undermines the rigorous characterization of the function-space operator setting.

The general-position assumption (distinct biases within each hidden layer) may be restrictive in practice. For example, zero-initialized biases (common in some architectures) violate it, and the theory predicts loss of universality in such regimes. While this is discussed, it reduces the practical reach of several main universality claims.

The paper is purely theoretical and does not provide empirical validation of the predicted phenomena (e.g., the benefit of larger input architectures for function-space operators), which is acknowledged but still limits the immediate applicability of the results.

Several key statements in the main text (Proposition 7.1, Theorem 7.2) are informal and their formal versions appear only in the appendix, making the main narrative harder to assess without consulting the supplement.

Some proofs rely heavily on prior results (e.g., [51], [41], [49]) and the paper does not fully reproduce the necessary conditions under which those results apply, leaving a small risk of hidden assumptions.

strengths: Develops an ambitious and unified theoretical framework for expressivity of permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, covering four natural approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators).
Introduces the general-position assumption (distinct biases in hidden layers) and shows it enables universality via a continuous canonization map, which is a natural and practically mild condition.

Provides constructive simulations proving expressive equivalence among several prominent architectures (DWS, NFN, GMN, NG-GNN), which unifies prior work and simplifies the landscape of weight-space networks.

Establishes both universality and non-universality results, including a limitation for fixed architectures when approximating function-space operators that increase geometric complexity, and shows that increasing architecture size overcomes this limitation.
The theoretical results, if correct, provide principled guidance for when existing permutation-equivariant architectures suffice and when more expressive designs are needed.
weaknesses: A central claimed contribution is that NFTs match the expressive power of other architectures under general position (Proposition 5.3, Proposition D.22). However, Definition D.12 of NFTs does not include the positional encoding (PE) for input/output neurons, while the proof of Proposition D.22 explicitly assumes that NFTs use the NP-NFN positional encoding to implement the 'first-layer per-neuron operator'. This internal inconsistency undermines the claimed equivalence for NFTs.

Several proofs are sketchy or contain technical errors. For example, in Lemma F.15 the sets U_i are defined as subsets of K but then claimed to be an open cover of B_{ε/4}(K); the partition-of-unity argument needs correction. Also, the definition of the neuron-identification map (Definition F.3) uses an undefined symbol \bar{\eta}_l^b(j), and some equations have typos (e.g., Eq. (186)).

The universality proofs rely heavily on cited results (e.g., Pacini et al. [51] for separation-to-approximation, Navon et al. [49] for forward-pass simulation, DeepSets universality [59]) without fully verifying that these results apply to the exact DWS architecture and the compact sets used. Some steps are hand-wavy, especially the approximation of the rank/sorting map by DWS networks.

The limitation result for function-space operators (Theorem F.9) considers a somewhat artificial class of operators satisfying a specific 'zoom-out' property on [a,b]^n. While illustrative, it does not provide a broad characterization of natural limitations, and the paper's claim of a 'comprehensive expressivity characterization' may be overstated.

The manuscript is dense and difficult to follow. The main text provides only proof sketches, and the appendix is very long with many technical lemmas, making independent verification challenging. Some definitions and notation are introduced only in the appendix, and the figures are small and not very informative.
No empirical validation is provided. While this is a theory paper, the practical implications (e.g., benefits of larger architectures for function-space operators) remain speculative and untested.

strengths: Provides a unified expressivity theory for permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, formalizing four natural approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, and permutation-equivariant operators) and systematically analyzing universality in each.

Proves expressive equivalence among major architectures (DWS, HNP-NFN, NP-NFN+PE, GMN, NG-GNN) via cyclic containment arguments, and extends equivalence to NFTs under a general-position assumption, unifying disparate prior results.

Establishes both positive and negative results: universality for function-space functionals (Theorem 6.1), non-universality for permutation-invariant functionals in full generality (Proposition 6.2), universality under GP (Theorem 6.3), non-universality for fixed-architecture function-space operators (Proposition 7.1), and universality with growing architecture (Theorem 7.2).
Develops useful technical tools such as neuron-identification, canonization via bias sorting, and pointwise MLP realization by DWS layers, with detailed constructive proofs in the appendix.

Clearly discusses limitations and practical implications, including low-precision/quantized regimes where the GP assumption may fail, and the need for architectures that can output weights of a different architecture.
Good scholarly positioning: connects to geometric deep learning expressivity literature, prior weight-space results, and summarizes the landscape in Figure 1.
No apparent ethical concerns; the work is theoretical and does not involve human subjects, sensitive data, or potential misuse.
weaknesses: Several appendix proofs are long and contain hand-wavy or potentially incomplete steps: e.g., the affine-extension argument in Theorem F.9 assumes each global linearity region intersects [a,b]^n in a full-dimensional set; Lemma F.7's concatenation of sorted terms is sketched rather than fully formal; and Theorem F.10 requires extending I∘Ψ from an open neighborhood to all of C(X,Y) without explicit justification.

The main text's proof sketches sometimes diverge from the formal appendix proofs (e.g., Theorem 6.3's sketch versus its reduction to Theorem 7.4), which may confuse readers and makes the logical structure harder to follow.

The non-universality results (e.g., Proposition 6.2) are proved for the equivalent non-NFT class, but the main text occasionally refers to 'invariant weight-space networks' broadly; since NFT can separate the constructed points in Proposition D.21, the scope of the negative result should be stated more precisely.

The general-position assumption (pairwise distinct biases per hidden layer) excludes networks without biases and may be violated in low-precision/quantized settings; while acknowledged, the theory's reach in such regimes is limited.
The equivalence results are about approximation closure on compact sets and do not quantify depth/width trade-offs between architectures, so practical guidance on architecture choice remains coarse.

No empirical validation of the theoretical predictions (e.g., improved approximation of function-space operators with larger input architectures) is provided; the paper acknowledges this as future work, but it leaves the practical significance of some results untested.

strengths: Provides a comprehensive and unified expressivity theory for permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, including a strong equivalence theorem among prominent architectures (DWS, NFN variants, GMN, NG-GNN).

Identifies four natural approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) and characterizes universality/non-universality in each with precise conditions such as the general-position assumption and sufficiently large input architectures.
Proofs are technically sophisticated and mostly rigorous, leveraging and extending tools like continuous canonization maps, DeepSets universality, and separation-to-approximation results.

The theory-driven Output Capacity Expansion (OCE) modification is simple yet effective, achieving SOTA on the standard MNIST INR dilation benchmark with up to 34% improvement over prior SOTA, and the ablation over ensemble size shows consistent gains while controlling total parameter count.
Extends the analysis beyond MLPs to transformer weight spaces in Appendix H, demonstrating broader applicability of the framework.
Includes an honest limitations discussion and considers alternative exclusion sets (e.g., p-norm based) with empirical validation of the general-position assumption.
weaknesses: The definition of NFT in Appendix D.12 does not include the neuron-type positional encoding that the proof of Proposition D.22 relies on; this inconsistency may undermine the claim that NFTs match other architectures under the general-position assumption and requires clarification.
The code link is missing (stated as 'available at .'), which hinders reproducibility despite otherwise detailed experimental settings.

The empirical evaluation is limited to a single task (MNIST INR dilation) and one type of operator; broader validation across different weight-space tasks and architectures would strengthen the practical claims.
Some notation is inconsistent (e.g., k vs. d for output feature dimension, 'cañon' vs. 'canon'), and the paper is dense with many appendix references, making it hard to follow in places.
The theoretical results are asymptotic (universality) and do not provide approximation rates or sample complexity, limiting practical guidance on how large architectures need to be.

The connection between Theorem 7.2 (large input architecture) and OCE (increased output capacity via an ensemble) is somewhat loose; the theory does not directly prove that OCE overcomes the limitation for a fixed input architecture.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-theorized question: the expressive power of permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, which is timely given the growth of weight-space learning.

The expressive-equivalence result (Theorem 5.2) unifying DWS, NP-/HNP-NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN into a single expressivity class is a clean and practically useful takeaway, and the NFT exception (Prop. 5.3) is handled carefully.

The four-setting approximation framework (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) is a well-organized and sensible taxonomy that helps structure an otherwise messy design space.

The negative result on function-space operators (Prop. 7.1 / Thm. F.9) is a nice, somewhat surprising limitation, and the companion positive result with growing capacity (Thm. 7.2) is a coherent story.
The empirical validation of the general-position assumption (Appendix G) is a thoughtful and honest addition that connects the theory to practical quantization regimes.

The OCE experiments show consistent, non-trivial improvements across two architectures, and beating a gradient-using baseline (ScaleGMN+GradMetaNet++) while using only weights is a genuine point in the method's favor.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the central proof techniques (canonization under a general-position assumption, the separation-to-approximation theorem of Pacini et al. 2025b, WL-indistinguishability arguments, and ReLU linear-region counting) are all standard in the geometric-deep-learning expressivity literature and are transferred here to a new domain. The equivalence theorem largely assembles existing pairwise simulation results (Navon et al., Lim et al., Kofinas et al.).

The general-position (GP) assumption does most of the heavy lifting. Under GP the neuron-permutation symmetry is effectively broken, so canonization-by-sorting makes universality almost immediate; the non-universality results (Props. 6.2, 7.3) only hold on a measure-zero exclusion set. The upshot is that the networks are universal 'except on measure-zero sets,' which is clean but largely expected and reduces the surprise of the characterization.

Empirical validation is thin and the headline claim is not rigorous. Results rest on a single benchmark (MNIST INR dilation). The '34% improvement over prior SOTA' compares against numbers taken verbatim from other papers with potentially different training setups; only DWS/GMN k=1 are reproduced under the authors' setup, so the SOTA comparison is not apples-to-apples. A rigorous claim would reproduce all baselines under one protocol and use more than one task.

OCE is a trivial modification (averaging k output networks) and its connection to the theory is loose. Theorem 7.2 concerns a single sufficiently large output architecture, whereas OCE averages k networks of the same size; the 'theory-guided' framing overstates the link. Ensembling outputs is a well-known technique, so the method's novelty is marginal.

Presentation is dense and heavily reliant on the appendix; key results (Prop. 7.1, Thm. 7.2) are only stated informally in the main text. The appendix contains typos and garbled/duplicated material (e.g., the 'DWS layers used for maximal expressivity' subsection in F.1, 'netowrk', inconsistent use of d vs. k), and figures are cluttered.

The 'comprehensive characterization' is limited to MLPs; transformers are only sketched in Appendix H and other architectures (CNNs, RNNs) are not covered, so the comprehensiveness claim is overstated.
Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link is left empty ('available at .'), and the mixed provenance of baseline numbers makes the empirical claims hard to verify independently.
Optimization and generalization are entirely out of scope (acknowledged), which is acceptable but further limits the practical reach of the claims.

strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive and unified expressivity theory for permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, resolving a fragmented landscape. It proves expressive equivalence of DWS, HNP-NFN, NP-NFN+PE, GMN, and NG-GNN (Theorem 5.2), and shows NFT is equivalent under general position (Proposition 5.3).

It introduces a clear taxonomy of four natural approximation settings and characterizes universality/non-universality in each: function-space functionals are universally approximable (Theorem 6.1); permutation-invariant functionals and permutation-equivariant operators are not universal in full generality (Propositions 6.2 and 7.3) but become universal under a mild general-position assumption (Theorems 6.3 and 7.4); and function-space operators require growing architecture capacity (Proposition 7.1 and Theorem 7.2).

The general-position assumption is natural and well-justified: the bias exclusion set has Lebesgue measure zero, is validated empirically on 60k MNIST INRs, and the paper discusses alternative exclusion sets and extends the framework to transformer weight spaces.

The theory-driven Output Capacity Expansion (OCE) modification is simple yet effective, achieving up to a 34% improvement over prior SOTA on the standard MNIST INR dilation benchmark (GMN+OCE: 1.06e-2 vs. previous SOTA 1.60e-2), with parameter-matched controls and consistent gains across ensemble sizes for both DWS and GMN.
The appendix is detailed, with full proofs, explicit constructions of canonization maps, and comprehensive experimental details (seeds, hyperparameters, compute), supporting the technical claims.
The paper is well-structured and clearly written for such a dense theoretical topic, with helpful figures (e.g., expressivity landscape and approximation settings) and an honest limitations section.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is hindered by a missing code link: the manuscript states that code, configurations, and logs are available at a blank URL, with no supplementary reference. Independent reproduction is therefore not straightforward.

Some technical proofs are terse and contain potentially inconsistent indexing/notation. For example, in Appendix F.3 the neuron-identification map defines η_ℓ^w(i) using η_{ℓ-1}^b(i) for 1<ℓ≤L and i for ℓ=1, while W_ℓ row indices belong to layer ℓ; this needs clarification/correction, as it affects the canonization construction in Lemma F.6 and F.7.

The empirical evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (MNIST INR dilation) and two base architectures (DWS and GMN). Broader validation across tasks, architectures, and weight-space operators would strengthen the practical claims.

The OCE method is essentially an ensemble/averaging modification. While theoretically motivated by Theorem 7.2, its architectural novelty is modest, and comparisons against methods that use additional signals (gradients, probes) are not fully apples-to-apples.

The universality results rely on a general-position assumption that fails in low-precision/quantized regimes, as the authors themselves show. This restricts the practical reach of the theory, though the paper is transparent about this limitation.
